_comment: Production series, film 3. Slides only (no recording); code and output of the loader of the complete example github.com/fundsxml/examples/tree/main/PostgreSQL_End_to_End.

description.en: How FundsXML files get into a database safely, with the loader of the complete PostgreSQL example: the steps of a robust loader, a landing folder, cheap checks first, triggers, validation and schema versions, idempotency through the UniqueDocumentID, full and delta deliveries, streaming large files with one handler per repeating element, funds and subfunds, the order of assets and positions, asset keys, transactions, documents and regulatory templates, business rules, speed, six deliveries and four broken files at work, corrections and deletions, reconciliation, code checks, error reports, tests and release. All files can be downloaded.

say.en: A FundsXML file has arrived. How does it get into the database, safely, even when it is large, and even when the same file arrives twice? In this film you see the steps of a robust loader, the traps on the way, and the loader of the complete example at work, on six deliveries and four broken files. You can download all of it.

A robust loader works in six steps, and the example follows them for every file in its landing folder. Check the file: is it complete, and from a known sender? Validate it against the schema. Register the delivery with its document ID; a document ID that is already known is skipped. Read the data and write it to the tables, in one transaction. Reconcile the result, and only then release it. A file that fails a check moves to the error folder, with a report next to it. The original file is never changed, and every step writes a line to the log.

en.title: The cheap check first

say.en: The first check is cheap. Is the file complete? A file cut off during transfer has no closing root element; the example reads only the last bytes of the file to find out. Does it come from an expected sender? The control data at the top of the file says so, and which schema version it declares. Zipped files are unpacked first. Only then does the expensive work begin.

items.head: File watcher
items.text: Starts as soon as a file arrives.

items.head: Schedule
items.text: Loads at fixed times.

items.head: Both
items.text: Load on arrival, alarm at the deadline.

say.en: When does the loader start? Either a watcher notices every new file and starts at once, or the loader runs at fixed times. The best of both: load as soon as a file arrives, and raise an alarm when a file has not arrived by its deadline. Then a late delivery is noticed in the morning, not at noon, when someone asks for the data.

items.head: Invalid: not loaded at all
items.text: Half a delivery is worse than none.

items.head: Keep the error report
items.text: With the file.

items.head: XSD 1.1
items.text: Saxon or Xerces.

say.en: Validate first, load later. A file that fails the schema is not loaded at all, not even partly, because half a delivery is worse than none. The error report is kept with the file, and the sender is told. Remember that FundsXML needs an X S D one point one validator, such as Saxon or Xerces.

items.head: A newer version than expected
items.text: Validate against it, load what you know, log the rest.

items.head: Nothing is lost
items.text: The original is in the archive.

say.en: Which schema to validate against? Against the version the file declares, as long as you know it. When a partner already sends a newer version, validate against that one, load the elements you know, and log the rest. The original file is in the archive, so nothing is lost; the new elements can be loaded later.

en.title: Twice is not double
en.code:
def register_delivery(cur, path, ctl):
    """Idempotency: a UniqueDocumentID we already have is skipped, never loaded twice."""
    cur.execute("SELECT status FROM delivery WHERE unique_document_id = %s",
                (ctl["unique_document_id"],))
    if row := cur.fetchone():
        return None, row[0]
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO delivery (unique_document_id, ..., file_sha256, raw) "
                "VALUES (%s, ..., XMLPARSE(DOCUMENT %s)) RETURNING delivery_id", ...)
    return cur.fetchone()[0], None

# AMEND / DELETE: replace_related() marks the rows of the related delivery as replaced

say.en: Files arrive twice more often than you think: a repeated transfer, a manual upload. So the loader registers every document ID, together with a hash and the original file. If the same ID comes again, it skips the file. If a delivery is a correction, it replaces the data of the delivery it names. That way, loading the same file twice never doubles the data.

items.head: Full
items.text: The complete state; replaces everything for that fund and date. Simpler, more robust.

items.head: Delta
items.text: Only changes; needs a complete start. Saves volume.

items.head: Agree it
items.text: The loader must know which one it reads.

say.en: Another question to settle with each partner: does a delivery contain the full state, or only the changes? A full delivery replaces everything the receiver knows for that fund and date. A delta delivery only adds and changes, and needs a complete start. Full deliveries are simpler and more robust; deltas save volume. Your loader must know which one it is reading.

items.head: DOM
items.text: The whole file in memory. Fine for prices and small portfolios.

items.head: Streaming
items.text: Element by element, any size: StAX in Java, iterparse in Python.

say.en: How to read the file? The simplest way loads the whole document into memory. That is fine for prices and small portfolios. But a delivery with thousands of positions, regulatory templates and embedded documents can reach hundreds of megabytes. Then read it as a stream, element by element: with StAX in Java, or iterparse in Python.

items.head: In the file
items.text: Positions first, AssetMasterData at the end.

items.head: Read twice
items.text: Assets first, then positions.

items.head: Or stage
items.text: Positions into a staging table, link at the end. The example loader does this.

say.en: Streaming has one catch. In FundsXML, the asset master data comes after the funds and their positions. So while reading a position, its asset is not known yet. Two solutions: read the file twice, assets first. Or write positions into a staging table and link them to their assets at the end. The example loader does the second.

en.title: One handler per repeating element
en.code:
self.handlers = {
    "FUND/SingleFundFlag":                      self.fund,
    "SUB/Currency":                             self.subfund,
    "FUND/SingleFund/ShareClasses/ShareClass":  self.share_class,
    "SUB/ShareClasses/ShareClass":              self.share_class,
    "…/Portfolios/Portfolio/Positions/Position": self.position,
    "…/PositionsDecomposed/Positions/Position":  self.look_through,
    "…/Transactions/Transaction":               self.trade,
    "FundsXML4/AssetMasterData/Asset":          self.asset,
    "FundsXML4/Documents/Document":             self.document,
    "…/EMT_V4_2/FinancialInstrument":           self.emt,  ...
}
for event, elem in etree.iterparse(path, events=("start", "end")):
    ...  handler(elem); elem.clear()     # handled, then thrown away

say.en: This is the core of the example loader. It walks through the file once and calls one handler for every repeating element: a fund, a subfund, a share class, a position, a trade, an asset, a document, a template record. Funds and subfunds have the same parts, so one name covers both levels. After each element, its memory is released, so neither the size of the file nor the number of funds in it matters.

en.title: Many funds, dates and natures in one pass

items.head: A stack of funds
items.text: The umbrella, then each of its subfunds.

items.head: A share class at a time
items.text: With all its prices, net assets, flows and distributions.

items.head: One row per date and nature
items.text: An ESTIMATED and an OFFICIAL price are two rows.

items.head: The month-end file
items.text: 5 funds, 264 prices, 522 positions, 209 trades: one pass.

say.en: Several funds in one file are no special case for such a loader. It keeps a small stack: the umbrella, and inside it the subfund it is reading. A share class arrives with all its prices, net assets, flows and distributions, and every price becomes a row with its date and its nature. The month-end file of the example, with five funds and more than a thousand records, goes through in one pass.

en.title: Finding the asset
en.code:
def asset_keys(asset, supplier):
    """Identifiers first. Without any, the key becomes supplier/asset type/ID."""
    keys = [(scheme, asset.findtext(f"Identifiers/{tag}")) for tag, scheme in ID_SCHEMES.items()]
    keys = [(scheme, value) for scheme, value in keys if value]
    if not keys:
        keys.append(("SUPPLIER", f"{supplier}/{asset.findtext('AssetType')}/"
                                 f"{asset.findtext('UniqueID')}"))
    return keys

def resolve_asset(cur, asset, supplier):
    """Find the asset by any of its identifiers, or create it."""
    ...  SELECT asset_id FROM asset_identifier WHERE (scheme, value) IN (...)
    ...  known: UPDATE asset (the latest master data wins)  /  new: INSERT, logged

say.en: Then the keys. For each asset, the loader looks for it by its I S I N, or by the key built from sender, type and the sender's own identifier. If it is unknown, it creates it. If it is known, it updates its master data with the newer values. New assets are counted in the log, because a sudden flood of new assets often points to a problem in the delivery.

items.head: Trades and income
items.text: Wait in memory for their assets, then rows.

items.head: Documents
items.text: Base64 decoded, size checked, hashed; linked to funds and classes.

items.head: Templates
items.text: EMT, EET, TPT: the record as XML, plus key fields.

say.en: The other parts follow the same pattern. Trades and income also refer to assets, so they wait until the asset master data has been read; there are few of them, so they wait in memory. Embedded documents are decoded, their size is compared with the size the file declares, and they get a hash. And every template record is kept as X M L, with its key fields as columns.

en.title: Template records: XML plus key fields

say.en: Here are the three templates of the example. Each handler names the template and its version, the share class or portfolio it reports on, and the few fields that are kept as columns: the ongoing costs of the E M T, the S F D R product type of the E E T, the number of positions of the T P T. A new template version needs a new line here, not a new table.

items.head: All or nothing
items.text: On an error everything is rolled back.

items.head: Bulk writes
items.text: Not row by row.

items.head: After a fix: just load again
items.text: The document ID prevents doubles.

say.en: Writing happens in one transaction per file. If anything goes wrong, everything is rolled back, and the database is as before. For speed, rows are written in bulk, not one by one. And after the cause of an error has been fixed, the file is simply loaded again; thanks to the document ID, nothing is doubled.

items.head: Schema error
items.text: Always rejected.

items.head: Business warning
items.text: e.g. a large price change: load, flag, ask.

items.head: Business error
items.text: e.g. weights of 120 %: hold back until corrected.

say.en: Not every problem is a reason to reject a file. A schema error always is. But a business warning, such as an unusually large price change, may be correct; load the data, flag it, and ask. A real business error, such as weights that add up to a hundred and twenty percent, holds the delivery back until the sender corrects it. Agree on these rules with your partners.

items.head: Bulk insert or COPY
items.text: Thousands of positions per second.

items.head: One fund at a time
items.text: Small memory, restart in the middle.

items.head: Speed is rarely the problem
items.text: Correctness is.

say.en: How fast can it be? With bulk inserts, or the copy command of PostgreSQL, a loader writes thousands of positions per second. Large tables load faster when some indexes are built after the load. And processing one fund at a time keeps memory small and lets you restart in the middle. Speed is rarely the real problem; correctness is.

say.en: Then a correction. The amend names the daily file it corrects; the loader marks all sixty-six prices and one hundred fourteen net asset values of that file as replaced, and loads the complete corrected data. A file sent by mistake is taken back by a delete: its rows are marked replaced, and nothing new is loaded. Nothing is overwritten; both stay in the history.

say.en: And the four broken files. The file cut off during transfer fails the cheap check, before any validation. The second copy of the daily file is skipped, because its document ID is known. The file from an unknown sender is rejected. And the file with two elements in the wrong order fails the schema. Six loaded, one skipped, three rejected, and the database is exactly as it should be.

say.en: And what is in the database now? A look with psql. Six deliveries, five funds, eleven share classes. Two hundred eighty-five net asset values and four hundred eighteen prices: that includes the rows replaced by the correction and the deletion, because nothing is overwritten. Four portfolios with five hundred twenty-two positions, four hundred thirty assets, two hundred nine trades, nine documents and twelve template records. Every number matches the log.

Before the data is released, reconcile it. Do the position values add up to the total net assets? Do the weights add up to one hundred percent? Are the counts plausible compared with the last delivery? The two subfunds and the two single funds of the month-end file all reconcile to the cent. The data-quality checks of FreeXmlToolkit do the same on the file; the loader repeats them on the data.

items.head: Every listed code
items.text: Against the lookup tables of the version.

items.head: From a newer version
items.text: Keep it, with a warning.

items.head: Otherwise unknown
items.text: An error: usually a mapping problem.

say.en: The loader also checks codes. Every listed code, such as a price nature or a document type, is compared with the code list of the schema version. A code from a newer version than the sender declares is kept with a warning. Any other unknown code is an error, because it usually means a mapping problem on the sender's side. Findings are stored with the delivery, and a delivery with errors is held back.

en.title: A report the sender can act on
en.code:
File:        wrong-order.xml
Document ID: EXAMPLE-AM-NAV-2025-11-05-ORDER
Rule:        SCHEMA
Details:     line 134: cvc-complex-type.2.4.a: Invalid content was found starting with
             element 'Currency'. One of '{Names}' is expected.
Outcome:     rejected, nothing was loaded. Please send a corrected file with a new
             UniqueDocumentID.

say.en: When a delivery fails, the sender needs a report it can act on. It names the file and its document ID, the rule that failed, where in the file, what was found and what was expected. And it says what happens now: the file was rejected, or loaded with warnings. A precise report gets a correction back in minutes, a vague one in days.

items.head: Realistic deliveries
items.text: Several funds, dates and natures.

items.head: Broken files
items.text: Cut off, invalid, unknown sender, a duplicate.

items.head: The generator's output loaded back
items.text: No new assets.

items.head: On every change
items.text: run_all.sh in CI.

say.en: Test the loader as carefully as the generator. Use realistic deliveries, with several funds, dates and natures. Add broken ones: a file cut off in the middle, an invalid file, a file from an unknown sender, a duplicate. Load the same files twice, then a correction, then a deletion. Load the generator's output back in. The example does all of this with one script, on every change.

en.title: Release
en.code:
SELECT release_delivery('EXAMPLE-AM-NAV-2025-11-05', 'data team');

 id  unique_document_id                 op       status    released_by  findings
  1  EXAMPLE-AM-MONTHEND-2025-10-31     INITIAL  released  data team           0
  2  EXAMPLE-AM-NAV-2025-11-05          INITIAL  released  data team           0
  4  EXAMPLE-AM-NAV-2025-11-05-AMEND-1  AMEND    released  data team           0
  6  EXAMPLE-AM-NAV-2025-11-06-DELETE   DELETE   released  data team           0

say.en: Only then is the data released. A status column on the delivery shows the way: loaded, checked, released. A function releases a checked delivery and records who did it, and when. Reports and downstream systems read only released data. Warnings go to the data team, who decide whether to release anyway or to ask the sender for a correction.

say.en: Everything you saw in this film is in the complete example: the loader, the six deliveries and the four broken files, the queries, and the script that runs it all. You find it in the FundsXML examples repository on GitHub, in the folder PostgreSQL end to end, also as a single zip file. Start a database, run the script, and watch the same log on your own screen.

That was loading FundsXML: validate first, never twice, streaming with one handler per repeating element, and reconcile before release. In the next film, you see the other direction: generating FundsXML from the same database. Thanks for watching.
